Prologue.

It is a well-known thing that the astrologers called Genethliaci are diligent in knowing the hour and exact moment of each person's birth: with this knowledge they divine and predict the natural inclinations of men, by consideration of the sign under which they are born, and of the state and aspect that the planets then had among themselves and in relation to the sign. These astrologers, or diviners, base their divination on the influence of the constellations and planets; and for this reason their divination is tolerated, and permitted in the almanacs that common people use, on the condition that no one should think that the influence of the constellation does anything more than incline one toward sensuality, and that it has no power whatsoever over free will.

The natives of all New Spain had, and still have, great diligence in knowing the day and hour of each person's birth, in order to divine the character, life, and death of those who were born. Those who held this office were called tonalpouhque, and to them people turned as if to prophets, whenever a son or daughter was born, to be informed about their character, life, and death. These diviners were not guided by the signs or planets of the sky, but by a set of instructions which, according to them, was left by Quetzalcoatl, which contains twenty characters multiplied thirteen times, in the manner set forth in the present book. This kind of divination cannot in any way be licit, because it is not based on the influence of the stars, nor on anything natural, nor does its cycle conform to the cycle of the year, since it contains no more than two hundred and sixty days, after which it begins again from the start. This device is either a continuous artifice, or an art of necromancy, or a pact and fabrication of the devil, which must be rooted out with all diligence.

To the sincere reader.

In the present volume, friend reader, you have all the movable feasts of the year in their order, and the ceremonies, sacrifices, rejoicings, and superstitions that were practiced on them; from which one may take indication and warning in order to know whether these are now observed wholly or in part — although, since the time at which they occur is not known, being movable feasts, it will be difficult to fall upon them exactly. You also have here a great deal of vocabulary pertaining to this subject, matter well worn among them but quite hidden from us. There is occasion in this subject matter to judge the ability of these people; it contains, though briefly, some rather delicate things, as can be seen in the table found at the end of the book.

Book Four

Book Four, of judicial astrology, or the art of divination, which these Mexicans used in order to know which days were well-fortuned and which were ill-fortuned, and what conditions those born on the days attributed to the characters or signs set forth here would have; and it seems to be a matter of necromancy rather than of astrology.

Chapter One, of the first sign, called Ce Cipactli, and of the good fortune that those born under it had — both men and women — unless they lost it through their own negligence or laxity.

Here begin the characters of each day, which were reckoned in periods of thirteen (trecenas): there were thirteen days in each "week," and they formed a circle of two hundred [and sixty days]...

[Parallel Nahuatl text:]

This is the fourth book: it speaks of the book of days (the tonalamatl), which the Mexica consulted for guidance; and thus said the day-counters — whether a day was good or not good — by it the fate of the day was signified, here it is called [as follows]: and what would befall the one who was born under it. And this book of days is, in truth, more properly called the tonalpohualli (count of days), by which especially they reckoned.

Chapter One: it speaks concerning the first sign, called Ce Cipactli, and of the good fortune merited by those born under it, men and women — unless they themselves lost it, bringing it upon themselves through their own laziness.

Here begins the count of days: just as a single week was counted, so thirteen days were made into one such period.

The thirteenth day is of another character, called acatl, which means "cane."

These thirteen days, they said, were very fortunate, so that whoever was born on any of these thirteen days—if he were the son of a nobleman—would be a lord or a senator, and rich. And if he were the son of humble fortune and poor parents, he would be brave, honored, and respected by all, and would have enough to eat. And if a girl were born on any of these thirteen days, she would be rich and would have everything necessary for her household: for spending on food and drink, for giving feasts, for dancing, and for holding gatherings in her house; and she would give food and drink to the poor, the elderly, and orphans who have nothing to eat or drink, and she would be prosperous...

[The accompanying Nahuatl text, corresponding to this Spanish passage, describes the same ideas in the original language: it speaks of becoming wealthy, being honored and served, having food and drink provided, being comforted in old age, and the good fortune — or in other cases, misfortune and suffering, including hardship, poverty, illness, and need — that could come to those born under these day-signs, according to Aztec belief in fate tied to the calendar.]

...what he did, by his work, in order to earn his living: and nothing of his labor will be lost to him: and he will be skillful at selling all kinds of merchandise, and at earning as much as he can. And moreover they said: that even though, at the moment of a child's birth, it had a very fortunate character, if it did not do penance, and if it was not corrected, and if it did not endure the punishments that are given to it, and the jealous and harsh words that are spoken to it—and if it is poorly raised and does not walk the straight path—it loses everything that it had deserved through the good sign under which it was born. Such a person despises himself and blinds himself, even if he takes up with a concubine. He loses the good fortune he had, and so he becomes poor, and has nothing to eat or drink, and will suffer great hardship all his life; because he himself brought misfortune upon himself through his own wickedness, being disobedient, arrogant, and careless. He will find contentment nowhere, and will always live in poverty and misfortune. Everyone will despise him, everyone will hold him as worthless, no one will take him as a friend, he will wander alone, no one will love him, and everywhere people will wish him ill and speak evil of him. ...they looked upon him with bad eyes, for being a notorious sinner, and everyone cursed him, for being proud and a vagabond, and for going about lost and disobedient to what he was commanded and counseled, and because he did not care for proper upbringing. And when a child was born under a good sign, the fathers and mothers would say: "Our child is fortunate, and has a good sign," which is called Cipactli.
Then they would baptize him, and give him the name of the sign: they would call him Cipac, or they would give him another name from among the grandparents, etc.
And if it seemed good to them, they would postpone the baptism to another day, so that it might fall under a better fortune, within the same sign. And if the child born was a boy: when they baptized him, they made him a small shield, with four little arrows, and they tied the umbilical cord to them, and gave it all together to men who were soldiers, so that they might carry it to the place of battle, and there they buried it. And if the child born was a girl: when they baptized her, they placed in a washbasin all the implements of a woman — those with which women spin and weave — because the life of a woman is to be raised at home, and to remain and live within it: her umbilical cord they buried near the hearth.

[Parallel Nahuatl text, describing the same matters concerning the day-sign Cipactli — the manner in which one born under it might become shameless, quick-tempered, a drunkard, or hardened in wrongdoing, unable to be corrected or counseled; and how, if someone born under a fortunate day within the sign of One Crocodile (Ce Cipactli) was bathed and given his fate, the rites of washing and naming were performed accordingly, whether a new house was to be dedicated or the child was to be bathed; and if a male child was born, at the time of his bathing a small shield was made for him, and four little darts, and these were bound to his umbilical cord and hung upon him, together with other things pertaining to his future estate...]

And this astrology, or necromancy, was taken and had its origin from a woman called Oxomoco, and from a man called Cipactonal. And the masters of this astrology, or necromancy, who kept count of these signs, who were called tonalpouhque [day-counters]: they painted this woman Oxomoco, and this man Cipactonal, and placed them in the middle of the books, where all the characters of each day were written; for they said that these two were the lords of this astrology, or necromancy, as the principal astrologers, because they had invented and made this count of all the characters.

The second character is called ocelotl, which means "tiger" [jaguar]: this one reigned for another thirteen days. They said it was an unfortunate sign during all the thirteen days it governed. This ocelotl held the first house, or day. The second held quauhtli, which means "eagle." The third held cozcaquauh, which means another large bird so called. The fourth held olin, which means "movement." The fifth held tecpatl, which means "flint." The sixth held quiauitl, which means "rain." The seventh held xochitl, which means "flower." ...[the Nahuatl text continues, describing] belongs to one ocelotl: and [it was said] it was not a good day-sign; one who was born in it, a woman, [would suffer] trouble; and by it the destiny was shown, one could not easily be cured of it. And whoever was born in it, nearly everyone, would turn out poorly.

Thus the thirteen-day period begins, named One Ocelotl. When it began, it was said it was not a good day sign, a sign of ferocity, a sign of seizing and taking captives, and there spread out the thirteen [day-signs] belonging to it: namely, two Eagle, three Vulture, four Movement, five Flint, six Rain, seven Flower, eight Crocodile (Cipactli), nine Wind, ten House, eleven Lizard, twelve Serpent, thirteen Death: and whoever was born under it, [it was said], a noble, or a commoner — it was said, [that it meant] death in war, destruction, captivity, imprisonment...

[It] means swordfish. The ninth sign had Ehecatl, which means wind. The tenth had Calli, which means house. The eleventh had Cuetzpalin, which means lizard. The twelfth had Coatl, which means serpent. The thirteenth had Miquiztli, which means death.

Whoever was born—whether noble or commoner—under any of these houses (signs), it was said that he would have to be a captive in war, and in all his affairs he would be unfortunate and vicious, and very given to women; and even if he became a brave man, in the end he would sell himself into slavery. And this he did because he was born under such a sign. But they also said that even though he was born under such an unlucky sign, he could remedy this through the skill and diligence he showed: by not sleeping much, doing penance, fasting, and piercing himself to draw blood from his body, and sweeping the house where he was raised,

It speaks of the sign Nahui Ollin (Four Movement), which was greatly venerated by Motecuhzoma; when this sign arose, incense was burned and offerings made before the image of the sun called Cuecaltonameyotl. And, the fast having passed, all bathed themselves in order to celebrate the feast of the said sign Seven Flower (Chicome Xochitl), and they said that this sign was also an unlucky one: that any woman weaver who broke the fast would become, and deserved to become, a public woman. And they said further that weaver-women were nearly all of bad conduct in their bodies, by reason of what happened, at the origin of weaving, with the goddess Xochiquetzal, who deceived them. And this goddess also gave them incurable scabs and pox, and other contagious diseases; and she who did penance, as she was obliged to, deserved to be a woman of good fame and honor, and would be well married.

And they said further that whoever was born under the said sign Flower (Xochitl) would be skillful in all the mechanical arts, if diligent and well brought up; and if not well brought up and understanding, neither would such a one deserve good fortune, but rather misfortunes and dishonors. Because some have been deceived, and even to this day the deception persists, concerning certain counts that these natives anciently used, I consider it worthwhile to set forth here an explanation of three kinds of counts that they used, and which are still used in some places.

The first count is the division of the year into its months. The case is that they divided the year into eighteen parts, and to each part they gave twenty days; these can be called months, so that their year had eighteen months, which together make three hundred and seventy days; and the five days that remain over, in order for the year to be complete, are not counted, but were called the idle and unlucky days, because they were dedicated to no god.

The purpose toward which they directed this division is that each month, or each twenty days, they dedicated to a god, and on those days they held feasts and sacrifices—except that in two of the months they held a feast for four gods, giving ten days to one and another ten to the other. And thus, keeping the eighteen months, the feasts they celebrated in them numbered twenty.

This count is called the calendar, in which all the days of the year are dedicated to the gods, except the five which, as has been said, they held as idle and unlucky days. This count, which is the calendar that these natives have kept since time immemorial, has nothing to do with the other two counts, which will be explained next.

The second count that these natives used is called the count of the years, because they counted a certain number of years in the following manner: they had four characters, placed in four positions around a round circle. One of these characters they called Ce Acatl, which means "one reed"; this character was depicted like a green painted reed, and in relation to the circle, it faced toward the east. As for the first thing it says, that by this reckoning the Indians counted six weeks, months, and years, this is utterly false; because this reckoning does not contain more than two hundred and sixty days, and lacks one hundred and five days to make up the count of a whole year; nor did they count their months by this reckoning, because their months number eighteen in a year, and each one has twenty days, which makes three hundred and sixty days — a number this reckoning does not reach. Nor do they count their weeks by this reckoning either, because what they say — that they had thirteen days per week — is false, for in that case one week would have thirteen days, and another week would overlap with three days into the following month; and thus each month would not have complete weeks — especially since their "weeks" were of five days, which would better be called "quintanas" rather than weeks, and there are four of these quintanas in each month. hill which is near Iztapalapan, which they call Huixachtécatl. And they
reached the summit about midnight, or nearly so, where there stood a solemn
temple built for that ceremony. Having arrived there, they watched the
Pleiades to see if they were in the middle of the sky, and if they were not
yet there, they waited until they arrived. And when they saw that the stars
had already passed the midpoint, they understood that the movement of the
heavens had not ceased, and that this was not the end of the world, but that
they would have another fifty-two years assured, in which the world would not
come to an end. At this hour, on the surrounding hills that encircle this
whole province of Mexico—Texcoco, Xochimilco, and Cuauhtitlan—there waited a
great multitude of people, expecting to see the new fire, for this was the
sign that the world would go on. And as soon as the priests drew the fire,
with great ceremony, in the temple on that hill, it immediately became
visible throughout all the surrounding hills; and those who stood watching
there at once raised a great shout.

...that they felt in their hearts such joy that the world would not end, and that they had another fifty-two years assured. The last solemnity that they held for this new fire was in the year one thousand five hundred and seven: they held it with full solemnity, because the Spaniards had not yet come to this land. In the year one thousand five hundred and fifty-nine, the other cycle of years ended, which they call Xiuhmolpilia (the binding of the years). And in this one they did not hold a public solemnity, because by then the Spaniards and the religious were already in this land. So that this present year of one thousand five hundred and seventy-six falls within the fifteenth year of the cycle of years now running. When they drew the new fire and performed this solemnity, they renewed the pact they had with the demon to serve him: and they renewed all the statues of the demon that they kept in their houses, and all the ornaments of his service, and those of their own houses: and they made great celebrations, knowing that now they had the world assured, that it would not end for another fifty-two years. It is clearly evident that this device of counting was an invention of the devil, in order to make them renew the pact they had with him every fifty-two years: and by frightening them with the end of the world, and making them believe that he was extending the time and granting them mercy by letting the world continue, [he kept them bound to him].

¶ Besides this reckoning, they also had a custom that every eight years they held a fast of bread and water for eight days, and at the end they held a festival in which they performed a solemn rite with various personages; in which they said that they discovered fortune (or that they deserved it), and they called it Atamalcualiztli.

¶ Another festival they held every four years, in honor of the fire, in which they pierced the ears of all the boys and girls, and called it Pillauanaliztli: and this festival seems very likely, and there are conjectures that it served as their leap-year adjustment, counting six "nemontemi" (unlucky days).

¶ The other reckoning of time is of one year, which they divided into eighteen months, and to each month they gave twenty days: and each of these months was dedicated to one or two gods: and they held their festivals within it. Each of these months was in turn divided into groups of five days each, and they held their market days on the last of these five days, in one town: and from there every five [days, in another town...]

¶ These natives had another count that does not follow the count of the year,
nor of the months, nor of the quintanas, which may be improperly called
weeks. This count has twenty characters, as is painted
on the table that is behind this leaf: to each one of these characters
they attributed thirteen days; during which one of these characters reigned: in such a
way that each one reigned for thirteen days, and the circle that these characters

has one hundred and five days fewer than a year. This count was used
to divine the conditions and outcomes of the life that those who were born
would have. It is a delicate count, and very deceptive, and without any
foundation in natural astrology. Because the art of judicial astrology,
which is used among us, has its foundation in natural
astrology, which is in the signs and planets of the sky, and in the courses

possible that any man could have fabricated or invented this art; for

Because the preceding table of the divinatory art is difficult to understand and to count: I have placed this table that follows, because it is much clearer and the reckoning much easier, and in accordance with how they themselves used to count. And let no one think that this table is a calendar, because, as has been said, it is not an [art] but rather the divinatory art. The calendar of these natives is placed at the beginning of the second book and is very clear to understand, because of the letters of the alphabet that it has: on one side, their own months are counted, which are of twenty days each. And on the other side, our months are counted, which are of thirty days, more or less. And because this reckoning is arranged in this way, it is easy to know on which of our months their feasts fall, and on which day of each month. The other reckoning, which is that of the years, is placed in the seventh book of this history; there it may be seen, God willing, when it comes to light.
